claim: Defense against infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is mediated by CD4 T cells.
source: Defense against infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is mediated by CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about Mtb immunity.

claim: CCR2+ inflammatory monocytes have been implicated in Mtb-specific CD4 T cell responses.
source: CCR2+ inflammatory monocytes (IMs) have been implicated in Mtb-specific CD4 T cell responses but their in vivo contribution remains unresolved.
evidence: This statement references prior research implicating IMs in CD4 T cell responses.

claim: Transient ablation of IMs during infection prevents Mtb delivery to pulmonary lymph nodes.
source: Herein, we show that transient ablation of IMs during infection prevents Mtb delivery to pulmonary lymph nodes, reducing CD4 T cell responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Transient ablation of IMs during infection reduces CD4 T cell responses.
source: Herein, we show that transient ablation of IMs during infection prevents Mtb delivery to pulmonary lymph nodes, reducing CD4 T cell responses.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in the manuscript.

claim: Transfer of MHC class II-expressing IMs to MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted recipients restores Mtb transport to mLNs.
source: Transfer of MHC class II-expressing IMs to MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted recipients, while restoring Mtb transport to mLNs, does not enable Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is a finding from adoptive transfer experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transfer of MHC class II-expressing IMs to MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted recipients does not enable Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming.
source: Transfer of MHC class II-expressing IMs to MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted recipients, while restoring Mtb transport to mLNs, does not enable Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is a finding from adoptive transfer experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transfer of MHC class II-deficient IMs corrects CD4 T cell priming in monocyte-depleted, MHC class II-expressing mice.
source: On the other hand, transfer of MHC class II-deficient IMs corrects CD4 T cell priming in monocyte-depleted, MHC class II-expressing mice.
evidence: This is a finding from adoptive transfer experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Specific depletion of classical DCs does not reduce Mtb delivery to pulmonary lymph nodes.
source: Specific depletion of classical DCs does not reduce Mtb delivery to pulmonary lymph nodes but markedly reduces CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is a finding from DC depletion experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Specific depletion of classical DCs markedly reduces CD4 T cell priming.
source: Specific depletion of classical DCs does not reduce Mtb delivery to pulmonary lymph nodes but markedly reduces CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is a finding from DC depletion experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: IMs acquire characteristics of DCs while delivering Mtb to lymph nodes.
source: Thus, although IMs acquire characteristics of DCs while delivering Mtb to lymph nodes, cDCs but not moDCs induce proliferation of Mtb-specific CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: cDCs but not moDCs induce proliferation of Mtb-specific CD4 T cells.
source: Thus, although IMs acquire characteristics of DCs while delivering Mtb to lymph nodes, cDCs but not moDCs induce proliferation of Mtb-specific CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by multiple experiments in the manuscript.

claim: Inflammatory monocytes express Ly6c, CD11b and CCR2.
source: Inflammatory monocytes (IMs) express Ly6c, CD11b and CCR2, a chemokine receptor that facilitates emigration of IMs from the bone marrow (Serbina and Pamer, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about IM phenotype, supported by citation.

claim: CCR2 is a chemokine receptor that facilitates emigration of IMs from the bone marrow.
source: Inflammatory monocytes (IMs) express Ly6c, CD11b and CCR2, a chemokine receptor that facilitates emigration of IMs from the bone marrow (Serbina and Pamer, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference (Serbina and Pamer, 2006).

claim: IMs make important contributions to innate immune defense during infection.
source: Although IMs make important contributions to innate immune defense during infection, recent studies also implicate IMs in priming of CD4 T cell responses during fungal, viral and parasitic infections (Traynor et al., 2000; Leon et al., 2007; Edismo et al., 2009; Hohl et al., 2009; Rivera et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations indicating prior research.

claim: Recent studies implicate IMs in priming of CD4 T cell responses during fungal, viral and parasitic infections.
source: Although IMs make important contributions to innate immune defense during infection, recent studies also implicate IMs in priming of CD4 T cell responses during fungal, viral and parasitic infections (Traynor et al., 2000; Leon et al., 2007; Edismo et al., 2009; Hohl et al., 2009; Rivera et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Traynor et al., 2000; Leon et al., 2007; Edismo et al., 2009; Hohl et al., 2009; Rivera et al., 2011).

claim: Experiments using CCR2-deficient mice suggested that monocytes contribute to T-cell-mediated defense against Mtb.
source: Experiments using CCR2-deficient mice also suggested that monocytes contribute to T-cell-mediated defense against Mtb.
evidence: This references prior experimental findings from CCR2-deficient mouse studies.

claim: IMs can serve as permissive host cells for Mtb in later stages of infection.
source: IMs, however, can also serve as permissive host cells for Mtb in later stages of infection, suggesting that IMs can both restrict and enhance Mtb infection (Antonelli et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Antonelli et al., 2010).

claim: IMs can both restrict and enhance Mtb infection.
source: IMs, however, can also serve as permissive host cells for Mtb in later stages of infection, suggesting that IMs can both restrict and enhance Mtb infection (Antonelli et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited reference (Antonelli et al., 2010).

claim: Recruitment of IMs in CCR2-deficient mice is defective throughout early, intermediate and late stages of infection.
source: Because recruitment of IMs in CCR2-deficient mice is defective throughout early, intermediate and late stages of infection, it has not been possible to specifically define the role of monocytes at different times during infection (Peters et al., 2001; Scott and Flynn, 2002; Peters et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Peters et al., 2001; Scott and Flynn, 2002; Peters et al., 2004).

claim: It has not been possible to specifically define the role of monocytes at different times during infection using CCR2-deficient mice.
source: Because recruitment of IMs in CCR2-deficient mice is defective throughout early, intermediate and late stages of infection, it has not been possible to specifically define the role of monocytes at different times during infection (Peters et al., 2001; Scott and Flynn, 2002; Peters et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of CCR2-deficient mice, supported by citations.

claim: CCR2-DTR mice were used to transiently deplete IMs during discrete stages of Mtb infection.
source: Therefore, we used CCR2-DTR mice to transiently deplete IMs and other CCR2-expressing cells during discrete stages of Mtb infection.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: Administration of DT to CCR2-DTR mice depletes inflammatory monocytes from the lung and mLN.
source: Administration of DT to these mice depletes inflammatory monocytes from the lung and mLN (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: CCR2-DTR mice that received three doses of DT surrounding the time of aerosol infection did not differ from control mice in terms of mycobacterial growth in the lungs.
source: CCR2-DTR mice that received three doses of DT surrounding the time of aerosol infection did not differ from control mice in terms of mycobacterial growth in the lungs (Figure 1A), indicating that CCR2-expressing cells are not required for the establishment of pulmonary infection following Mtb inhalation.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CCR2-expressing cells are not required for the establishment of pulmonary infection following Mtb inhalation.
source: CCR2-DTR mice that received three doses of DT surrounding the time of aerosol infection did not differ from control mice in terms of mycobacterial growth in the lungs (Figure 1A), indicating that CCR2-expressing cells are not required for the establishment of pulmonary infection following Mtb inhalation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CD4 T-cell priming occurs approximately 7–10 days following inhalational challenge.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that CD4 T-cell priming occurs approximately 7–10 days following inhalational challenge (Wolf et al., 2007; Gallegos et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Wolf et al., 2007; Gallegos et al., 2008).

claim: Depletion of CCR2-expressing cells 7, 9 and 11 days following infection resulted in a threefold increase in the number of live Mtb in the lungs on day 15.
source: Depletion of CCR2-expressing cells 7, 9 and 11 days following infection resulted in a threefold increase in the number of live Mtb in the lungs on day 15 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Monocyte-depleted and control mice had similar Mtb CFUs in lungs 12 days following infection.
source: Although monocyte-depleted and control mice had similar Mtb CFUs in lungs at this time (Figure 1C), Mtb CFUs were markedly reduced in mLNs of mice treated with DT (1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mtb CFUs were markedly reduced in mLNs of mice treated with DT 12 days following infection.
source: Although monocyte-depleted and control mice had similar Mtb CFUs in lungs at this time (Figure 1C), Mtb CFUs were markedly reduced in mLNs of mice treated with DT (1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Reducing live M. tuberculosis transport from the lung to the draining lymph node following monocyte depletion on days 7–11 post infection might delay priming of Mtb-specific CD4 T cells.
source: We reasoned that reducing live M. tuberculosis transport from the lung to the draining lymph node following monocyte depletion on days 7–11 post infection might delay priming of Mtb-specific CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: mLNs obtained from monocyte-depleted mice were smaller, with significantly reduced total and CD4 T cell numbers compared to PBS treated mice.
source: In comparison to mLNs obtained from PBS treated mice, mLNs obtained from monocyte-depleted mice were smaller, with significantly reduced total and CD4 T cell numbers (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: C7 T cells had proliferated in mLNs of control mice 12 days after infection but had not expanded in monocyte-depleted mice.
source: C7 T cells had proliferated in mLNs of control mice 12 days after infection but had not expanded in monocyte-depleted mice (Figure 2B,D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and 2D.

claim: Reduced C7 T cell proliferation in mLNs resulted in reduced C7 T cell frequencies in lungs of monocyte-depleted mice 21 days following infection.
source: Reduced C7 T cell proliferation in mLNs resulted in reduced C7 T cell frequencies in lungs of monocyte-depleted mice 21 days following infection (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: Transfer of naïve C7 T cells to control mice resulted in a four to fivefold reduction of Mtb CFUs in lungs.
source: Transfer of naïve C7 T cells to control mice resulted in a four to fivefold reduction of Mtb CFUs in lungs, suggesting that supplementing the endogenous T cell repertoire with additional naive, ESAT-6-specific CD4 T cells enhances immune defense against Mtb infection (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Supplementing the endogenous T cell repertoire with additional naive, ESAT-6-specific CD4 T cells enhances immune defense against Mtb infection.
source: Transfer of naïve C7 T cells to control mice resulted in a four to fivefold reduction of Mtb CFUs in lungs, suggesting that supplementing the endogenous T cell repertoire with additional naive, ESAT-6-specific CD4 T cells enhances immune defense against Mtb infection (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Depletion of monocytes abrogated enhanced protection resulting from addition of naive C7 T cells.
source: Depletion of monocytes abrogated enhanced protection resulting from addition of naive C7 T cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Subsets of NK cells, dendritic cells and CD4 T cells can express CCR2.
source: Although IMs represent the most prevalent CCR2-expressing cell population, subsets of NK cells, dendritic cells and CD4 T cells can also express CCR2.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CCR2 expression patterns.

claim: IMs were purified from CCR2-GFP mice by sorting GFP+ cells that did not express NK1.1, CD4, FLT3 and C-kit, yielding a highly purified (>99% pure) population of IMs.
source: To exclude the possibility that depletion of a non-monocyte cell population resulted in loss of Mtb transport from lungs to mLNs, we purified IMs from CCR2-GFP mice by sorting GFP+ cells that did not express NK1.1, CD4, FLT3 and C-kit. This strategy did not require antibody staining for trafficking molecules (CCR2 and CD11b) and eliminated NK cells, CD4 T cells, dendritic cell progenitors and hematopoietic stem cells, yielding a highly purified (>99% pure) population of IMs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The transferred IMs were detectable in lungs and mLNs.
source: The transferred IMs were detectable in lungs and mLNs and down-regulated expression of CCR2 and CD11b and up-regulated expression of MHC class II, CD11c and CD103 during trafficking from the lung to mLNs (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Transferred IMs down-regulated expression of CCR2 and CD11b during trafficking from the lung to mLNs.
source: The transferred IMs were detectable in lungs and mLNs and down-regulated expression of CCR2 and CD11b and up-regulated expression of MHC class II, CD11c and CD103 during trafficking from the lung to mLNs (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Transferred IMs up-regulated expression of MHC class II, CD11c and CD103 during trafficking from the lung to mLNs.
source: The transferred IMs were detectable in lungs and mLNs and down-regulated expression of CCR2 and CD11b and up-regulated expression of MHC class II, CD11c and CD103 during trafficking from the lung to mLNs (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: Administration of IMs to monocyte-depleted CCR2-DTR mice enhanced live Mtb transport to mLNs 12 days following infection.
source: Administration of IMs to monocyte-depleted CCR2-DTR mice enhanced live Mtb transport to mLNs, as detected 12 days following infection (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Infusion of IMs to WT mice did not enhance delivery of Mtb to mLNs.
source: Infusion of IMs to WT mice did not enhance delivery of Mtb to mLNs, suggesting that IMs are not limiting during the first 2 weeks of Mtb infection.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: IMs are not limiting during the first 2 weeks of Mtb infection.
source: Infusion of IMs to WT mice did not enhance delivery of Mtb to mLNs, suggesting that IMs are not limiting during the first 2 weeks of Mtb infection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation.

claim: Adoptive transfer of IMs to monocyte-depleted CCR2-DTR recipient mice rescued priming of C7 T cells.
source: Adoptive transfer of IMs to monocyte-depleted CCR2-DTR recipient mice rescued priming of C7 T cells (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Wild-type and CCR2-deficient IMs were equivalent at delivering Mtb to mLNs.
source: Quantitative culture 12 days following Mtb infection demonstrated that wild-type and CCR2-deficient IMs were equivalent at delivering Mtb to mLNs, indicating that CCR2-signaling does not contribute to trafficking of IMs between these sites (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: CCR2-signaling does not contribute to trafficking of IMs from infected lungs to mLNs.
source: Quantitative culture 12 days following Mtb infection demonstrated that wild-type and CCR2-deficient IMs were equivalent at delivering Mtb to mLNs, indicating that CCR2-signaling does not contribute to trafficking of IMs between these sites (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: C7 T cells were not primed in MHC class II-deficient recipients of MHC class II-expressing monocytes.
source: In contrast to our previous experiments with MHC class II-expressing recipients, C7 T cells were not primed in MHC class II-deficient recipients of MHC class II-expressing monocytes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Adoptively transferred IMs trafficked to mLNs in MHC class II-deficient recipients.
source: Adoptively transferred IMs trafficked to mLNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and, as demonstrated in the previous experiments, corrected Mtb delivery to draining lymph nodes to levels seen in mice that had not been monocyte-depleted (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Adoptively transferred IMs corrected Mtb delivery to draining lymph nodes to levels seen in mice that had not been monocyte-depleted.
source: Adoptively transferred IMs trafficked to mLNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and, as demonstrated in the previous experiments, corrected Mtb delivery to draining lymph nodes to levels seen in mice that had not been monocyte-depleted (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The magnitude of the C7 T cell response was similar in monocyte-depleted mice rescued with either MHC class II-expressing or deficient monocytes.
source: Figure 4C demonstrates that the magnitude of the C7 T cell response was similar in monocyte-depleted mice rescued with either MHC class II-expressing or deficient monocytes.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: IMs primarily serve as carriers of Mtb, delivering live bacteria to mLNs and enabling but not directly priming CD4 T cells.
source: Taken together, these experiments indicate that IMs primarily serve as carriers of Mtb, delivering live bacteria to mLNs and enabling but not directly priming CD4 T cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experiments in the manuscript.

claim: Classical DCs in lymph nodes and their progenitors express the cDC-specific transcription factor zbtb46.
source: Classical DCs in lymph nodes and their progenitors express the cDC-specific transcription factor zbtb46, whereas IMs do not.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DC markers.

claim: IMs do not express the cDC-specific transcription factor zbtb46.
source: Classical DCs in lymph nodes and their progenitors express the cDC-specific transcription factor zbtb46, whereas IMs do not.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IM markers.

claim: Depletion of classical DCs resulted in markedly reduced C7 T cell expansion.
source: Depletion of classical DCs resulted in markedly reduced C7 T cell expansion (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) but did not reduce the number of live Mtb in mLNs (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Depletion of classical DCs did not reduce the number of live Mtb in mLNs.
source: Depletion of classical DCs resulted in markedly reduced C7 T cell expansion (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) but did not reduce the number of live Mtb in mLNs (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: FLT3L-deficient mice lack classical DCs but not IMs.
source: FLT3L-deficient mice, which lack classical DCs but not IMs, also have markedly reduced CD4 T cell responses following Mtb infection (Figure 4F) despite the presence of Mtb in the mLN (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is established knowledge about FLT3L-deficient mice.

claim: FLT3L-deficient mice have markedly reduced CD4 T cell responses following Mtb infection.
source: FLT3L-deficient mice, which lack classical DCs but not IMs, also have markedly reduced CD4 T cell responses following Mtb infection (Figure 4F) despite the presence of Mtb in the mLN (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: FLT3L-deficient mice have Mtb present in the mLN despite reduced CD4 T cell responses.
source: FLT3L-deficient mice, which lack classical DCs but not IMs, also have markedly reduced CD4 T cell responses following Mtb infection (Figure 4F) despite the presence of Mtb in the mLN (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Classical DCs are dispensable for trafficking of live Mtb from infected lungs to mLNs.
source: These results indicate that classical DCs, while dispensable for trafficking of live Mtb from infected lungs to mLNs, are essential for CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DC depletion experiments.

claim: Classical DCs are essential for CD4 T cell priming during Mtb infection.
source: These results indicate that classical DCs, while dispensable for trafficking of live Mtb from infected lungs to mLNs, are essential for CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DC depletion experiments.

claim: During the second week of murine infection, IMs play the critical role of delivering live Mtb to draining mLNs.
source: During the second week of murine infection, IMs play the critical role of delivering live Mtb to draining mLNs, an indispensable step for Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in the manuscript.

claim: Delivery of live Mtb to draining mLNs is an indispensable step for Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming.
source: During the second week of murine infection, IMs play the critical role of delivering live Mtb to draining mLNs, an indispensable step for Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in the manuscript.

claim: IMs serve as transporters of live bacteria from the site of infection to the site of T cell priming.
source: Our results extend previous reports that IMs influence CD4 T cell priming (Leon et al., 2007; Hohl et al., 2009; Nakano et al., 2009; Rivera et al., 2011) by demonstrating that IMs serve as transporters of live bacteria from the site of infection to the site of T cell priming.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in the manuscript, extending prior cited work.

claim: IMs fail to prime DCs during Mtb infection despite acquiring characteristics of DCs.
source: In contrast to reports from other disease models demonstrating that IMs differentiate into DCs and then directly prime CD4 T cells (Cheong et al., 2010; Zigmond et al., 2012) our adoptive transfer studies using MHC class II KO mice reveal that IMs, despite acquiring characteristics of DCs, do not prime Mtb-specific CD4 T cells in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MHC class II KO adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: Evidence that moDCs generated in vitro can stimulate T cell responses suggests that IMs can process and present antigen.
source: Evidence that moDCs generated in vitro can stimulate T cell responses suggests that IMs can process and present antigen (Schreurs et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Schreurs et al., 1999).

claim: Several hundred adoptively transferred IMs were recovered from the mLNs of infected mice.
source: Recovery of several hundred adoptively transferred IMs from the mLNs of infected mice also suggests that sufficient numbers of IM were present to prime T cells.
evidence: This is an observation from the adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: IMs, by virtue of being infected with Mtb, may be ineffective at stimulating Mtb-specific lymphocytes, in contrast to resident dendritic cells that have not been infected.
source: One possible explanation is that IMs, by virtue of being infected with Mtb, are ineffective at stimulating Mtb-specific lymphocytes, in contrast to resident dendritic cells that have not been infected (Wolf et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors, with a supporting citation.

claim: Multiple DC subsets can be involved in priming of naive T cells.
source: A number of studies, however, have demonstrated that multiple DC subsets can be involved in priming of naive T cells (Itano et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Itano et al., 2003).

claim: CD103+ DCs play a role in transport and priming during CD8 T cell responses to cutaneous viral infection with potential contributions by inflammatory monocytes.
source: Other studies characterizing CD8 T cell responses to cutaneous viral infection have demonstrated a role for CD103+ DCs in transport and priming with potential contributions by inflammatory monocytes (Bedoui et al., 2009; Edismo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Bedoui et al., 2009; Edismo et al., 2009).

claim: IMs carry fungal antigens from a site of cutaneous inoculation to draining LNs and transfer antigens to LN resident DCs.
source: One previous study has suggested that IMs carry fungal antigens from a site of cutaneous inoculation to draining LNs and transfer antigens to LN resident DCs (Ersland et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the citation (Ersland et al., 2010).

claim: IMs transport bacteria to lymph nodes and transfer antigen to classical dendritic cells prior to CD4 T cell priming during live pulmonary infection with Mtb.
source: Our study extends this finding to live pulmonary infection with Mtb. IMs transport bacteria to lymph nodes and transfer antigen to classical dendritic cells prior to CD4 T cell priming.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experiments in the manuscript.

claim: Cross-dressing may play a role during Mtb infection.
source: It is possible that cross-dressing (Wakim et al., 2011), in which infected cells pass MHC molecules to uninfected cells, plays a role during Mtb infection.
evidence: This is a speculative possibility proposed by the authors, with a supporting citation.

claim: Transfer of MHC class II molecules from host cells to adoptively transferred, MHC class II-deficient monocytes was not detected.
source: We did not detect transfer of MHC class II molecules from host cells to adoptively transferred, MHC class II-deficient monocytes.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: The number of MHC/peptide complexes required per APC to stimulate T cell responses may be very small and below the level of detection.
source: The number of MHC/peptide complexes required per APC to stimulate T cell responses, however, may be very small and below our level of detection.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for why MHC transfer might not have been detected.

claim: Transfer of MHC class II molecules in either direction plays a minimal role in T cell priming during Mtb infection.
source: That said, given our finding that MHC class II-deficient IMs effectively complemented monocyte-depleted, MHC class II sufficient mice while MHC class II-expressing monocytes could not correct deficient T cell priming in MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted mice, we believe that transfer of MHC class II molecules in either direction plays a minimal role in T cell priming during Mtb infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MHC class II adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: M. tuberculosis Erdman was grown in 7H9 media.
source: M. tuberculosis Erdman was grown in 7H9 media, and log phase cultures were diluted to 8 × 106 bacilli per millimeter and sonicated before infection with an aerosol exposure system (Glass-Col).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: The aerosol exposure system was calibrated to deliver approximately 100 CFU per animal.
source: The volume of suspension, and exposure time were calibrated to deliver ∼100 CFU per animal.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: Inflammatory monocytes were harvested from the bone marrow of CCR2-GFP mice.
source: Inflammatory monocytes were harvested from the bone marrow of CCR2-GFP mice.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: 2 × 10^6 purified IMs per mouse were injected via the tail vein.
source: The cells were re-suspended in PBS and 2 × 10 (Kipnis et al., 2003) cells per mouse were injected via the tail vein.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: Statistical validation was done with the Student's t test.
source: Statistical validation was done with the Student's t test.
evidence: This describes the statistical methods used.

claim: p<0.05 were considered significant.
source: p<0.05 were considered significant, p>0.05 were considered insignificant.
evidence: This describes the statistical criteria used.
